rows.title: nobody knows when
rows.hook: one unstable nucleus is a surprise. a whole crowd of them follows a pattern. isn't that neat?

blocks.text: ok so take one unstable nucleus. leave it alone. it has a chance of changing, and nobody can say when. eep, so mysterious~
nobody pushes it. the nucleus that changes is the parent. the nucleus it becomes is the daughter. the change gives off radiation
a half-life ticks for a crowd of atoms, never for one
think of a die
roll a die once and you can't say if it will show a six. roll it 600 times and you can say that about 100 of the rolls will. hehe
a nucleus is like that. one is a surprise. a big group follows a pattern, and in the half-life lesson you'll see the pattern for yourself. it's so pretty~

blocks.caption: The radiation sign, used to mark a source of radiation.

blocks.text: Heating, cooling and chemistry hardly change how fast an unstable nucleus changes. In a flame or in ice, it is still unstable.

items: One nucleus: you can't say when
A big group: it follows a pattern

blocks.text: so when someone asks you when an atom will change, you can say: you can't know. a crowd of them, though, you can know. hehe, tiny mystery solved~

blocks.label: see what comes out of a decay

rows.title: the banana on your counter
rows.hook: a banana is a little bit radioactive. so are you. that's normal, and here's why

blocks.text: ok here's something nobody expects. the banana on your counter is a little bit radioactive. surprise~
it holds potassium, and a tiny share of that potassium is potassium-40, which is unstable. you carry some too, in your own body
it was here first
radioactivity wasn't invented. it was here long before people were. you can find it in four places

items: Rocks and soil: uranium and thorium
The air: radon, a radioactive gas from the ground
Space: cosmic radiation, all the time

blocks.caption: A banana holds a little natural potassium-40.

blocks.text: radioactivity was always here. we only learned to see it

In 1896 Henri Becquerel left a uranium mineral on a wrapped photographic plate. The plate fogged, even with no sunlight. Radioactivity was found in a natural mineral, long before anyone made nuclear technology.
is it dangerous?
radioactive doesn't automatically mean dangerous. what matters is the type of radiation, how much there is, and how it reaches the body.
a banana and your own body are radioactive, and that's normal. later you'll learn why being exposed to radiation isn't the same as becoming radioactive.

blocks.label: find where radioactivity hides around you

rows.title: The smallest thing you will ever meet
rows.hook: You have never seen one, yet you are made of them. Let us look at how small they really are.

blocks.text: Look at your hand. Now look at the air around it. Both are matter, and all matter is made of atoms.

Yes, even the air, which gives every impression of being nothing. That is why a pumped-up ball is heavier than a flat one: the air inside it is matter too. I have weighed several balls to be certain. The neighbours have asked me to stop.
Small things are best looked at slowly. I still look at them every day.
How small is small?
Take a skin cell. You need a microscope to see it. A virus is about 300 times smaller than that cell. And an atom is about 300 times smaller again.

blocks.caption: An atom: far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.

items: An atom: a few tenths of a nm

blocks.text: About 2,400 years ago the Greek thinker Democritus imagined cutting something in half again and again, until he reached a piece that could not be cut. He called it atomos. Seeing atoms took far longer.
Light and heat are different. They are energy, not matter, so they are not made of atoms.
So the next time you pick something up, remember that you are holding a huge crowd of atoms you can never see. Take a moment with that. I will wait.

blocks.label: Zoom in on an atom yourself

rows.title: Three kinds of carbon
rows.hook: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are all carbon. One of them is not like the others. Let us see which.

blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. Three atoms are all carbon, yet they are not the same. How can that be? Let us count.
Count the protons. Every carbon atom has 6, and that number is what makes it carbon. Change it and you get a different element.
The neutrons are the difference
The number after the name is the mass number: protons plus neutrons. Carbon has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons. I checked the subtraction. Twice.
These versions of one element are called isotopes. Most of the atoms around you are stable isotopes.
Isotope does not mean radioactive. It only means a different number of neutrons.
Carbon-14 is the unstable one. An unstable nucleus can change, and when it does it gives off radiation. That is called radioactivity.
Even so, nothing here is strange or new. Unstable atoms are in rocks, in the air and in food, and they were here long before us. The rocks have been very patient about it.
Which brings a question. What exactly comes out when a nucleus changes? Ada knows. She tells it brightly. Please be prepared.
